sidebarDescription: See how properties provide method-like behavior through field-like syntax, and compare explicit backing fields with C# 3.0 auto-properties.
connection: Session 05 introduced named methods and their boundaries. This optional sidebar uses that mental model to explain property accessors: get and set contain method-like behavior, while callers use the convenient syntax of reading or assigning a field.
objectives: Distinguish a field, a backing field, a property, and an auto-implemented property.
Explain how get and set provide method-like behavior behind field-like calling syntax.
Use the setter's value keyword to receive the value being assigned.
Recognize that auto-implemented properties arrived in C# 3.0 in November 2007.
Choose an explicit backing field when an accessor needs custom behavior.

visuals.title: A property controls access
visuals.explanation: Callers read and assign the property as if it were a field, while get and set define what happens at that boundary.

visuals.title: Accessors behave like methods
visuals.explanation: Reading a property invokes its get accessor. Assigning a property invokes its set accessor and supplies the assigned value through the value keyword.

visuals.title: Explicit and automatic storage
visuals.explanation: An explicit property names its private backing field. An auto-property asks the compiler to create inaccessible storage and simple accessors.

visuals.title: The public contract stays simple
visuals.explanation: Both forms expose the same ClockIn property to callers, so storage details can remain inside the class.

preQuiz.prompt: When code assigns entry.ClockIn = time, which accessor receives time?
preQuiz.explanation: Assignment invokes set. Inside that accessor, the special value keyword represents time.

preQuiz.prompt: What does an auto-property remove from code you must write?
options: The explicit backing field and trivial accessor bodies
preQuiz.explanation: The compiler supplies hidden storage and the simple get/set implementations.

preQuiz.prompt: When is an explicit backing field useful?
options: When an accessor needs validation or other custom behavior
Whenever a class has a constructor
preQuiz.explanation: A named backing field gives custom accessor code a place to read or store the value.

concept.title: A field is storage; a property is controlled access
paragraphs: A field is a variable declared directly inside a class. It stores data. A property is a class member that controls how callers read or assign a value.

Properties look like fields at the call site, but their accessors contain executable behavior. This is why method-like behavior with field-like syntax is a useful mental model. More precisely, properties are first-class C# members whose accessors compile to methods.
concept.code:
entry.ClockIn = new DateTime(2026, 8, 5, 9, 0, 0); // invokes set
DateTime start = entry.ClockIn;                    // invokes get

concept.title: The older explicit backing-field form
paragraphs: Before auto-implemented properties, a simple property required a field plus complete get and set bodies. The private field stores the value; the public property defines the class's external contract.
Inside set, value is a special implicit parameter containing the value on the right side of the assignment. The name _clockIn is an ordinary private-field naming convention, not special C# syntax.

concept.title: C# 3.0 introduced auto-properties
paragraphs: Auto-implemented properties were introduced with C# 3.0 in November 2007, alongside Visual Studio 2008 and .NET Framework 3.5.

When no custom accessor behavior is needed, the shorter declaration asks the compiler to create a hidden backing field and trivial accessors. Code inside the class cannot refer to that compiler-generated field by name.

concept.title: The caller uses both forms the same way
paragraphs: Changing from an explicit property to an auto-property does not change ordinary caller syntax. Both are assigned with = and read through the property name.
Use an auto-property for plain storage. Use an explicit backing field when get or set needs validation, normalization, logging, lazy calculation, or another deliberate behavior.

rows: Rare simple data shapes where uncontrolled access is intentional
A hidden field generated by the compiler
Simple property storage without custom accessors

labs.objective: Write the older property form one piece at a time so the storage and accessor behavior remain visible.

Paste the lab comment at the top of the file.

Inside the class, declare a private DateTime field named _clockIn.

postQuiz.prompt: Why is a property reasonably described as method-like behavior with field-like syntax?
options: Its get and set accessors execute behavior, while callers read and assign it by name
Every property is a public field
postQuiz.explanation: The accessors contain behavior, but caller syntax resembles reading or assigning a field.

postQuiz.prompt: What does value mean inside a set accessor?
options: The value being assigned by the caller
postQuiz.explanation: value is the setter's implicit input and contains the right side of the assignment.
C# 3.0 introduced auto-implemented properties in November 2007.

reflections: Which parts of the explicit property become hidden when you use an auto-property?
Why might validation justify keeping an explicit backing field?
Why is a property not the same thing as a public field, even when their caller syntax looks similar?
whatBreaks: Skipping this optional side lab does not break the required TimeClock path. You would only lose the side-by-side practice of tracing an assignment through set, storage, and get.
summary: A property exposes method-like get and set behavior through field-like caller syntax. Explicit properties use a backing field you declare; C# 3.0 auto-properties, introduced in November 2007, let the compiler generate hidden storage for simple accessors.
